items.title: Ezekiel 37 Prophecy About Israel’s Return Sparks Colton Dixon’s Latest Hit
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Interesting.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Singer Colton Dixon’s new song “Bones” comes at a time when the world feels, in many ways, like it’s on fire. The catchy tune is inspired by the valley of dry bones prophecy in Ezekiel 37.

Many Bible experts believe this chapter references Israel’s return to the land in 1948, and Dixon — who agrees — told CBN News some of his other reasons for connecting these Scriptures to “Bones.”

“It was kind of like the… the push to get off the sidelines as a believer, and to start prophesying over the dead things in my life,” he said of the song’s inspiration. “It comes from Ezekiel 37. … God gives Ezekiel a vision, brings him out into the middle of a desert full of a valley of dry bones, and tells him to start prophesying.”

Dixon continued, “So, as Ezekiel starts to prophesy, the bones start to rattle, they come together, and a whole army stands up around him.”

The singer believes the moment was prophetic for Israel “coming back and regaining their stance.” But he said the meaning can also run deeper, noting that Ezekiel’s hard-hitting message inspired him.

“As a believer, I’m like, ‘Man, I feel like we have this authority, spiritually, to prophesy over the dead things in our life,'” he said. “Galatians talks … about God getting us the keys to the kingdom. Whatever we bind on earth shall be bound in heaven. Whatever we loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. So I’m like, ‘All right, it’s time to stop sitting on the sidelines as a believer.'”

Dixon said it’s easy for Christians to fall into what he described as an “autopilot lifestyle” — something he wants to help people navigate.

“That’s not the way God designed it,” he said, comparing it to a car’s autopilot feature. “It’s a great feature for your car, I might add, but that’s not the way God designed us to … live our lives. You’re just going to miss out on God’s best for you doing it that way.”

He’s hoping “Bones” gets people thinking more about the importance of living out biblical truth.

“God has something incredible for you,” Dixon said. “And I don’t want to settle for…bad or good when I can have God’s best.”

items.title: Scholar Reveals New Josephus Analysis, Insight for Jesus’ Miracles and Resurrection
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Fascinating.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A college professor is revealing research he says helps corroborate early, extrabiblical writings about Jesus.

Dr. Thomas C Schmidt, associate professor of religious studies at Fairfield University, recently released, “Josephus & Jesus: New Evidence for the One Called Christ,” a book he believes helps set the record straight on Flavius Josephus’ writings.

“Josephus is one of the most important sources we have on the New Testament because he mentions so many people that are discussed in the New Testament, folks like Herod the Great, Herodias, Pontius Pilate, Caiaphas, Herod Agrippa, John the Baptist,” Schmidt said of the Jewish historian. “He talks about all these people, and he also talks about Jesus.”

But the professor said Josephus’ Jesus passage is “very controversial,” because many scholars have questioned the authenticity of this particular portion of the writings.

“They’ve thought that Christians tampered with it later on,” he said. “They thought Josephus didn’t actually write this. Josephus is writing in the first century. He was born in Jerusalem, raised in Jerusalem. So if he does tell us about Jesus, it would be the earliest witness to Jesus outside of Christian writings, which should just make it extraordinarily valuable and interesting.”

Schmidt said the majority position among scholars in the 19th century was that Josephus didn’t write any of the words about Jesus attributed to him and that the text was “completely fraudulent.”

“But then this brilliant scholar who was translating Josephus’ works, he started noticing that there were just many phrases in this account of Jesus that are odd phrases, but that Josephus himself uses many times elsewhere,” he said. “The scholar’s name was Henry Thackeray, and he turned the tide of arguments so that scholars started thinking, ‘Well, OK, clearly Josephus did say something about Jesus, but maybe Christians doctored it later on,’ because the belief by scholars was that what Josephus said was just too positive, too glowing to be written by a non-Christian.”

In the 21st century, scholars again looked at Josephus’ stylistic choices and found even more parallels between what was written about Jesus and Josephus’ other writings.

Schmidt conducted his own investigation for the book — and came to some fascinating conclusions.

“I exhaustively leverage these databases, and I show that every single phrase in the paragraph can be indexed back to Josephus in some way or another,” he said. “It sounds exactly like him. The turns of phrase, the vocabulary, everything sounds like Josephus.”

Schmidt said he also noticed something else in the passages some claim are “too pro-Christian.” One comment by Josephus is that Jesus worked miracles — something widely seen as supporting the Christian narrative. Schmidt said it’s more complex.

“Josephus says that Jesus worked miracles,” he said. “But the original Greek word is not quite so positive. It does mean ‘supernatural deeds’ but maybe we could better translate as ‘paranormal deeds.'”

Schmidt continued, “Josephus is acknowledging that Jesus worked supernatural deeds, but he’s unclear where the source of Jesus’ power is coming from. He doesn’t know if it’s malevolent, demonic — if it’s divine. In other words, Josephus looks like he’s assessing Jesus the same way the non-Christian Jews in the Gospels are responding to Jesus’s miracles.”

The academic said he started his journey writing “Josephus & Jesus: New Evidence for the One Called Christ,” on a quest to figure out how the Jesus passage had been changed by Christian scribes, adding that he initially agreed with the position that it wasn’t original.

“I was hoping that I could figure out what was changed so I could reconstruct what Josephus said,” he said. “But when I started looking at the results of these database searches, I became convinced that really the whole thing comes from Josephus.”

The resurrection is just one of the issues Schmidt addressed in his research.

“Traditionally, that part of the passage is translated as Josephus saying Jesus appeared alive again on the third day,” he said, noting that understanding the original language helps comprehension. “So, in other words, Josephus is not claiming that Jesus was resurrected. What he’s reporting is that the first disciples of Jesus claimed that Jesus was resurrected.”

And considering Josephus likely had access to people who put the disciples to death, he had remarkable first-hand information.

“Josephus didn’t just know people who knew the apostles; he knew people who knew Jesus, who were at his trial,” Schmidt said. “That’s the argument I make towards the end of my book. … I did not intend my book to be an argument in favor of Josephus’ passage being totally authentic, but that’s where the evidence led me.”

You can download, “Josephus & Jesus: New Evidence for the One Called Christ,” for free.

items.title: Doubt Isn’t the Opposite of Faith — But Certainty Might Be
items.author: Bruce Miller
items.summary: Maybe you believe in God, but you’re not sure how to respond when someone asks why you do. You call it absolute truth, but you’re not absolutely sure about it. At times, you may have your own doubts about God and Christianity. You probably know someone who is “deconstructing” their faith. They grew
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Maybe you believe in God, but you’re not sure how to respond when someone asks why you do. You call it absolute truth, but you’re not absolutely sure about it. At times, you may have your own doubts about God and Christianity.

You probably know someone who is “deconstructing” their faith. They grew up in church, went to a Christian school or were even in ministry, but now they’re not sure what they believe. They’re questioning the very foundations of their faith, and it’s uncomfortable and unnerving.

Let me lower your expectations right from the start. You probably won’t get every question answered, and your doubts won’t be eradicated. That’s OK.

Accepting Christian truths blindly doesn’t build thick faith. The old bumper sticker that declared, “God said it, I believe it and that settles it,” may have seemed helpful, but it has weakened faith.

Each of us has to take ownership of our faith. Believing something simply because someone told you has no depth, and the realizations we uncover on our own terms have the potential to transform our lives. Fyodor Dostoyevsky wrote, “I believe in Christ and confess him not like some schoolboy; but my hosanna has passed through a great furnace of doubt.” From the refining fire of doubt, strong convictions can emerge, forged by pursuing answers to our hard questions.

Doubt often gets a bad reputation, especially in church settings, but it can be productive. It can paralyze us, but it can also propel us to seek truth. Seasons of deep doubt and earnest questioning have shaped me spiritually. Questioning has the power to open minds, give rise to new ideas and reveal new horizons.

When the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak a global pandemic on March 11, 2020, it rocked the world. Instead of going to school, work or church, we sheltered in place. The simple act of hugging a family member, or even being in the same room with them, went from a show of affection to a potential threat to their health. Our mental health deteriorated. According to the World Health Organization, the global prevalence of anxiety and depression jumped by 25%.

The pandemic also had an unavoidable impact on people’s thoughts about God. According to the Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, “During the early months of the pandemic, Google searches for prayer relative to all Google searches rose by 30%, reaching the highest level ever recorded.” The researchers estimate that by as early as April 1, 2020, more than half of the world’s population had prayed for an end to the pandemic. The deaths of loved ones spawned doubt about a good God.

Even before the pandemic, nearly everyone, including me, went through seasons of wrestling with serious doubts about their faith. That questioning often leads a person deeper into God. Theologian Paul Tillich wrote, “Doubt is not the opposite of faith; it is an element of faith.”

Embrace your doubts, ask your questions and seek out truth. Not every question you ask will have a clear answer.

Mystery abounds in this life, and some spiritual realities exceed our understanding. But I agree with theologian Peter Abelard when he said, “Constant and frequent questioning is the first key to wisdom…. For through doubting we are led to inquire, and by inquiry we perceive the truth.”

Even if you aren’t struggling with doubts right now, it’s easy to dismiss someone else’s questions. You may want to tell them to quit worrying and accept that there are some things we will never understand. And when you’re the one asking, it’s tempting to busy yourself with work, family and hobbies to avoid the issue.

It’s easier than ever to dodge serious questions by retreating into our ever-present screens instead of engaging the life around us. Dismissing someone’s fears, or hiding from your own struggles, doesn’t help anyone.

I surfaced from my struggle with doubt, during dark days of doctoral work, with a new epistemological humility. After examining many other points of view in the history of ideas, I accepted the limitations of human knowledge. There is much we cannot know. We don’t know exactly how our bodies extract all the nutrients from the food we eat, but we know enough to eat healthy food. We don’t know everything about life or why some things happen, but we can know enough to develop a relationship with the living God.

Our doubts can drive us to discover God’s reality, and, more importantly, to experience God’s love in Christ, forging a solid faith. Even with lingering doubts and a lack of absolute certainty, we can be confident enough to love God and love others.

Excerpt taken from “The 7 Big Questions: Searching for God, Truth, and Purpose.” Used with permission from Bruce B. Miller.

items.title: Evangelization Is Our Responsibility
items.author: Mark Bradford
items.summary:
Mark Bradford

We can either pass by those in need, or we can embrace our neighbor in friendship and with the ministry of love that Jesus has entrusted to all of us who bear his name.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Mark Bradford

Those who attend Mass during the week know that through the fall we have been feasting on the richness of Luke’s Gospel, which unfolds the remarkable pattern of Jesus’s messianic mission first proclaimed in the fourth chapter.

After his baptism and temptations in the desert, Jesus returns to his hometown in Nazareth where we find a crowd gathered to hear him. Luke tells us, 

He stood up to read, and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,
because he has anointed me
to bring good news to the poor.
He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives
and recovery of sight to the blind,
to let the oppressed go free,
to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”

When he finished, “The eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him, all eyes were fixed on him,” and he said to them, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16–21). Their initial response to him was admiration, but that quickly turned to rage when he reminded them that God’s grace has never been confined to those who believed they were entitled to it. His examples of Elijah and Elisha ministering to Gentiles resulted in their trying to kill him. Belonging, it seems, is no guarantee that one will understand or welcome God’s salvific work. 

After Jesus escapes the mob, he returns to Capernaum and resumes his ministry, and in Luke’s Gospel, the miracles come rapidly, one after the other, as testimony that his claim in the synagogue in Nazareth was true. Soon, Jesus expands his circle by choosing twelve men as his apostles whom he entrusts with a share in his mission. Luke tells us that “Jesus called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal” (Luke 9:1–2).

But sometime after the apostles returned from their first venture, there was some confusion among them. John approached Jesus with a complaint. He said, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” Jesus’s response to him was, “Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you” (Luke 9:49–50). In his hometown of Nazareth, Jesus himself was an insider rejected by his own people. Now we have Jesus affirming the work of this anonymous exorcist who acts in the name of Jesus, but the apostles regard him as outside their circle. 

That scene is rich. If the apostles were thinking that their ministry was exclusive, they learned a lesson in humility that day. Luke does not tell us how this man came to act in Jesus’s name. We can only guess that he was acting on his own initiative—not casting out demons by his own authority but by the power of Jesus’s name. What he does tell us is membership in the apostles’ inner circle was not the condition Jesus imposed for allowing his work to flourish—there is a place for others.

John’s complaint about this man came immediately after the apostles were arguing among themselves over which of them was the greatest. Jesus “was aware of their inner thoughts” and resolved the dispute by bringing a little child into their midst to teach them that the key to ministry is humility: “The least among all of you is the greatest” (Luke 9:48). 

After Jesus announces his messianic mission in chapter 4, he begins to expand his circle to share his ministry with others, including spiritual gifts that would give witness to their preaching. Jesus calls his apostles and commissions them to go out to preach and heal in his name. Later in chapter ten, he appoints seventy others and sends them out in pairs as additional “laborers into his harvest.” 

In our own time, the Second Vatican Council affirmed the vocation of the laity in their Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity, Apostolicam Actuositatem. They wrote that, “The laity derive the right and duty to the apostolate from their union with Christ the head,” and “they are assigned to the apostolate by the Lord Himself” (3). 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

In one of his most revered parables, Jesus discusses with a Jewish lawyer what he must do to inherit eternal life. The lawyer provides the right response: to love the Lord with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and your neighbor as yourself. But Jesus responds to the lawyer’s question about who his neighbor is with a fantastic story of an injured man who had fallen into the hands of robbers and was left on the road beaten, robbed, and half dead. In the story, the religious figures—a priest and a Levite—both passed by him, making sure to cross to the other side of the road to avoid him. But a Samaritan, an outsider, stopped to care for this man. 

Jesus gives no indication of the injured man’s identity, and he only identifies the one who helped him as a Samaritan. As St. John says in his Gospel, “Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans” (John 4:9), but this Samaritan’s deep compassion becomes the central lesson in the story: Our neighbor is anyone in need, and when we see another person in need we must help—without distinction. The “insiders” failed in their obligation to the law, and the “outsider” provided a vivid reminder of what love really entails. 

The Roman Catholic Church has built an incredible network of support through its social services, and we Catholics can be tempted to assume that the charitable institutions of the Church will manage our charitable works for us. The anonymous exorcist makes clear that the Church’s institutional work does not replace our personal obligation to be evangelists.

There are many people near to us—even in our parishes—who still await an encounter with Jesus’s liberating mercy. The poor, unemployed, and homeless are waiting for relief from the burden of their poverty. Those who are captive to sin long for an encounter with the mercy of Christ, and the sick, disabled, and impaired search for welcome and friendship. The anonymous exorcist, the Good Samaritan, and Vatican II all show us that ministry isn’t the responsibility of a select few who hold positions within the institutional Church. Evangelization—bringing the good news of the messiah into the darkness of the current age—is all our responsibility.

Jesus presents us with an example of the demand of discipleship in the parable of the good Samaritan, and he leaves us with a choice. We can either pass by those in need, as the priest and Levite did, or we can embrace our neighbor in friendship and with the ministry of love that Jesus has entrusted to all of us who bear his name.

items.title: WOF 548 | The Meaning of Catholic Ordination
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Why do Catholics uphold this difference between what we call clergy and laity, and where does it come from?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Welcome back to the Word on Fire Show. I’m Matthew Petrusek, senior director of the Word on Fire Institute and the host of the Word on Fire Show. Thank you for joining us. One of the fundamental dividing lines within Christianity is marked by a disagreement about whether certain people (specifically men, within Catholicism) not only have a distinctive calling or vocation to serve the Church but are able to do so by means of ordination—that is, in a way that fundamentally or, to use philosophical language, ontologically distinguishes them from the flock they serve. Why do Catholics uphold this difference between what we call clergy and laity? Where does this distinction originate, and how can it respond to the critique that it is inegalitarian, elitist, and even sexist? Put more positively, what is it that bishops, priests, and deacons—the only ordained ministers within Catholicism—can contribute to the life of faith and the path toward salvation that no one else can? Here to explain the nature and meaning of ordination and the process by which it takes place, and to reflect on his recent experience ordaining new deacons into the Catholic Church at St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome, is Bishop Robert Barron.
